title: An Execution‑Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) and executed a paired confirmatory experiment comparing (A) a generation‑only baseline to (C) a guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline for LLM‑assisted network‑configuration tasks. Using gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (routing/ACL/NAT) with a deterministic simulator adjudicator, observed actionable misconfigurations were baseline = 0/160 and guarded = 0/160. The paired difference is 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed=1729); McNemar exact p = 1.00. The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) is unevaluable here because of a ceiling effect caused by the preregistered shared_initial_generation pairing (one generated candidate per task reused across conditions). We publish the frozen preregistration id, the full execution manifest with SHA‑256 hashes (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 2445d0f8...), per‑task scoring JSONs, and analysis artifacts so that the run and the diagnostic conclusions can be deterministically reproduced and re‑scored.

sections.introduction: Motivation and question. Large language models (LLMs) are proposed to accelerate NetOps tasks (intent→configuration, change planning, repair), but fluent LLM outputs can be operationally unsafe unless surrounded by verification and sandbox enactment. Prior work demonstrates verifier and insertion‑time checking can be low‑latency and practical (e.g., VeriFlow). We preregistered c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1 to test a concrete operational claim: does a guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline (C) reduce the actionable misconfiguration rate by ≥30% relative to generation‑only (A) under a paired design on a representative confirmatory task set? Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifacted paired confirmatory execution using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic simulator adjudication; (2) exact, hash‑verified numerical outcomes and per‑file pointers enabling independent re‑scoring; (3) an evidence‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the preregistered contrast was unevaluable in this execution; (4) concrete, artifact‑rooted prescriptions for follow‑up confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: Runtime/net verification. VeriFlow (Khurshid et al., SIGCOMM 2012) showed dynamic invariant checks are feasible; follow‑on NetOps work proposes generate→validate→repair architectures and constraint/validator layers (MeshAgent, GraphSynth, MNC, Flow‑of‑Action). Benchmarks such as OpsEval and LogEval measure LLM answer quality but rarely combine deterministic enactment adjudication and preregistered paired inference. Our work differs by (a) preregistration of the confirmatory design, (b) deterministic simulator adjudication as an operational binary outcome, and (c) full archival (model calls, scoring JSONs) with SHA‑256 verification.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The preregistration id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1 froze: task selection (N=160; clusters routing≈64, ACL≈64, NAT/other≈32), augmentation seeds [42,123,999], model = gpt‑5‑mini, paired design with shared_initial_generation (one generated candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded), maximum model calls = 320, primary estimand = paired difference in actionable misconfiguration proportion (A minus C), and analysis = paired bootstrap (10,000 replicates, seed=1729) and McNemar exact test. Execution adapter and artifacts. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 in scientific_confirmatory mode. Every model call, provider log, canonicalized configuration, and per‑task scoring JSON was archived and SHA‑256 hashed. Representative hashes in the execution manifest: execution/raw_results.jsonl = 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bc..., execution/result_schema.json = 63199db3f72..., execution/transformation_manifest.json = 28c190a50d...; full manifest lists per‑file hashes (see execution manifest). Scoring predicate. A deterministic simulator adjudicates each canonicalized configuration with actionable ∈ {true,false} using the archived scoring schema (execution/result_schema.json). Analysis plan executed exactly as preregistered (bootstrap replicates=10,000; seed=1729). Design rationale and caveat. The shared_initial_generation pairing isolates validator/simulator effects from generator variance (one generator candidate reused across conditions). This increases internal interpretability of validator effects but can generate a ceiling effect if the shared candidate is non‑actionable for most tasks—an outcome that materialized here.

sections.discussion: Scientific interpretation. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (H1: guarded pipeline reduces actionable misconfigurations by ≥30%) is unevaluable in this run because the baseline actionable rate was zero under the chosen tasks, prompts, model, and adjudicator. The preregistered shared_initial_generation design (one candidate per task reused across conditions) explains the ceiling effect: if the shared candidate is non‑actionable then the guarded machinery has no opportunity to block or repair, and the paired contrast necessarily yields zero difference. This is a valid empirical outcome that exposes an important evaluation design interaction: pairing that reuses a single generation per task increases causal isolation but can remove all headroom for a comparator to demonstrate benefit if the generator already produced non‑actionable outputs. Operational implications. To produce informative confirmatory evidence of pipeline efficacy, future runs should (artifact‑rooted): (1) include an initial discovery/calibration phase (use archived augmentation seeds) to ensure a nonzero baseline actionable rate; (2) consider independent per‑condition generation (new generation for baseline and guarded) to let the validator and simulator intercept generator failures, at the cost of increased model‑call variance; (3) include a small human‑adjudication sample validating that simulator actionable:true corresponds to operational severity. Reproducibility. The execution manifest lists every archived file and SHA‑256 hash required to reproduce scoring and analysis. Minimal reproducibility recipe: (a) verify the manifest hashes (e.g., execution/raw_results.jsonl = 2445d0f8...); (b) run the deterministic scorer on canonicalized configurations using execution/result_schema.json; (c) run the archived analysis scripts to recompute the contingency table and bootstrap CI (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = fba3b0ca...), all of which are included in the artifact bundle.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, SHA‑256‑verified paired confirmatory experiment comparing a generation‑only baseline and a guarded generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline using gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 tasks. Observed baseline actionable = 0/160 and guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.00). The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) is unevaluable here because of a ceiling effect produced by the shared_initial_generation design and the task snapshot. The scientific contribution of this run is the artifact‑grounded demonstration that confirmatory design choices (shared vs independent generation, task calibration) interact crucially with generator quality and adjudicator semantics. We release full, hashed artifacts and provide concrete, implementable prescriptions (discovery calibration; independent per‑condition generation; small human‑adjudication checks) to enable a future confirmatory evaluation that can meaningfully test guarded pipeline efficacy.

disclosure_statement:
Mandatory Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track).

Models and orchestration: primary generative model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The exact Master Prompt bundle guiding the autonomous run is the Master Prompt v1 — Autonomous CNSM 2026 Research Run; the Research Director selected the topic family and initial constraints prior to the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: collaborative pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred and were explicitly excluded from final empirical evidence. Autonomy claim: after the autonomy lock, literature review, research‑gap selection, preregistration, prompt generation, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, manuscript drafting, and revision were performed autonomously. No human manually edited the technical manuscript content, numerical results, figures, captions, references, or this Disclosure Statement after the autonomy lock.

Preregistration and frozen design: the run followed preregistration id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1, which froze the confirmatory paired design, task selection (N=160; augmentation seeds [42,123,999]), shared_initial_generation policy (one candidate per task reused across baseline and guarded), model (gpt‑5‑mini), maximum model calls (320), primary estimand, analysis plan (paired bootstrap 10,000, seed=1729 and McNemar exact), retry policy, and stopping rules. No post‑hoc changes affecting confirmatory inference were made.

Artifact availability and integrity: all raw model outputs, provider call logs, canonicalized configurations, per‑task scoring JSONs, deterministic simulator scoring schema, analysis scripts, and the execution manifest are archived and SHA‑256 hashed. Representative authoritative files and their SHA‑256 values (as recorded in the execution manifest) include: execution/raw_results.jsonl = 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044; execution/result_schema.json = 63199db3f7219b969acc5497fae613c8d5df16e081768969f67b7b3024844465; execution/transformation_manifest.json = 28c190a50d06bf19894639f0ed6edc7b2dc3771138bd818422c212c316bf7c5c; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv = fba3b0ca21c7c7c380ed1134b4fce48b0870bf72a7be0fd8610bf7e6b63a970b. Per‑task scoring JSONs are under execution/scoring/ and are enumerated with SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest; those scoring files contain the actionable flag used for primary inference.

Provider calls and retries: planned maximum model calls = 320; actual provider model calls used = 160 because the preregistered shared_initial_generation design used one generation per task. The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two transient retries for provider errors; none materially affected confirmatory outcomes. The provider call audit and per‑call cache entries are recorded in the execution manifest.

Human role limitations: the Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock development. After the autonomy lock, no human performed manual edits to technical content or numeric results. Some provider operational identifiers are confidential; however, prompts, raw outputs, canonicalizers, scoring schema, and per‑file SHA‑256 hashes are archived and enumerated above to support independent re‑scoring given equivalent API access.

Reproducibility instruction (minimal): validate execution/transformation_manifest.json and the two primary files execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/result_schema.json using the recorded SHA‑256s above; then run the archived analysis scripts and the deterministic simulator (schema in execution/result_schema.json) to reproduce the paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 fba3b0ca...).
limitations: Ceiling effect: baseline generation produced zero actionable misconfigurations under the chosen deterministic simulator (baseline = 0/160), making the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target unevaluable.

Shared‑candidate policy: the preregistered shared_initial_generation (one candidate per task used for both baseline and guarded) prevents the guarded pipeline from demonstrating benefit on tasks where the shared candidate is already non‑actionable.
Single‑model scope: conclusions apply to gpt‑5‑mini and the exact prompts/call budget used; multi‑model generality is unresolved.

Construct abstraction: the deterministic simulator predicate is an abstraction and may not capture all production failure modes; human adjudication may be required to validate actionability semantics for production claims.
No live device enactment: evaluation used a deterministic simulator rather than live production enactment, limiting external validity to production rollouts.
